questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between a linear data structure and a non-linear data structure? Give one example of each.
questions.a: Linear data structures arrange elements in a sequential order where each element has a unique predecessor and successor (except first and last), e.g., array, stack, queue, linked list. Non-linear data structures arrange elements hierarchically or in a network where an element can be connected to multiple others, e.g., tree, graph. A wrong answer (e.g., "linear means sorted, non-linear means unsorted") reveals confusion between logical arrangement and physical ordering; the student is conflating data organization with data values.

questions.q: A student says: "An array is a dynamic data structure because we can add elements to it by writing code like `arr.append(5)` in Python." Is this statement correct? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. In the context of data structure classification (as per NCERT), an array is a **static** data structure because its size is fixed at compile time / declaration and cannot be changed during runtime in languages like C/C++. Python's `list` is a dynamic array implementation that handles resizing internally, but the abstract data structure "array" is static. A wrong answer reveals the student is confusing the high-level language feature (Python list) with the fundamental data structure concept (static vs dynamic memory allocation).

questions.q: You are designing a system to manage the "Undo" functionality in a text editor. Which data structure would you choose and why? Explain the principle it follows.
questions.a: A **stack** is the appropriate data structure because the Undo operation must reverse the most recent action first (Last In, First Out – LIFO). Each user action (typing, delete, format) is pushed onto the stack; when Undo is pressed, the top action is popped and reversed. If the student chooses queue (FIFO), they misunderstand the temporal order required — undo must revert the latest change, not the earliest.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the memory representation of a static array and a linked list. How does this difference affect insertion at the beginning?
questions.a: A static array uses contiguous memory locations; inserting at the beginning requires shifting all existing elements one position right (O(n) time). A linked list uses non-contiguous memory (nodes linked by pointers); inserting at the beginning only requires creating a new node and updating its `next` pointer to the current head (O(1) time). A student who says "both are O(1)" ignores the shifting cost in arrays; a student who says "linked list is always faster" ignores the extra memory overhead per node and lack of cache locality.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "A tree is just a special case of a graph." Is this true? Justify your answer with reference to the definitions of both data structures.
questions.a: Yes, it is true. A graph is a collection of vertices (nodes) and edges connecting them, with no restrictions on cycles or number of parents. A tree is a connected, acyclic graph where each node (except root) has exactly one parent. Thus, every tree is a graph, but not every graph is a tree. A student who says "no, they are completely different" fails to recognize the hierarchical relationship in the mathematical definitions.

questions.q: Create a real-world scenario (not from the textbook) that requires a **queue** data structure. Describe the entities, the operations performed, and why FIFO is essential.
questions.a: Example: A hospital emergency room triage system. Patients (entities) are enqueued upon arrival with a priority tag (but within same priority, FIFO). Operations: `enqueue` (new patient arrives), `dequeue` (doctor calls next patient), `peek` (view next patient without removing). FIFO is essential because medical ethics and fairness demand that patients with the same urgency are treated in order of arrival. A poor answer would describe a stack-like scenario (e.g., "undo button") or a scenario where priority alone decides (ignoring FIFO within priority).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A data structure is a ______ format for organizing, processing, retrieving, and storing data in a computer's memory so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are ______ a contact list app for your phone.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can classify any given data structure as linear or non-linear, primitive or non-primitive, static or dynamic, and justify the classification with examples.
